It keeps close to the wording of the original and uses the established English of Anglo-Latin legal, liturgical and canon-law formulae. It is an aid to reading the original, not a published translation. div.head: ECf retr 36.4
div.ab: Quodsi interfectori defecerint iudices et testes, et dirationatum fuerit, quod [in]iuste sit interfectus, interfector dabit uadimonium iusticie episcopi et fideiussores inueniet rectum prosequendi.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 667 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page; the words in bold are the Retractator’s changes to ECf, as Liebermann prints them.
The square brackets in “[in]iuste” are Liebermann’s: the manuscripts read “iuste”, only Ph “iniuste” (note 23).

seg.hi: Umstand des Gerichts, welches jenen hingerichtet hatte (wohl nicht Eideshelfer oder Zeugen, die gegen ihn ausgesagt hatten)

note.seg: the bystanders of the court which had executed him (probably not oath-helpers or witnesses who had testified against him)
vgl. 2, 9. 8, 2. Der weltliche Richter hat bereits (36, 2) Pfand empfangen
cf. 2, 9. 8, 2. The secular judge has already (36, 2) received a pledge
Super instead of Quodsi — defecerint Lond

div.ab: But if the slayer lacks judges and witnesses, and it is deraigned that he was [un]justly killed, the slayer shall give a gage to the bishop's justice and shall find sureties for prosecuting the right.
